questions.q: How does this lesson's column-level GRANT example implement least privilege?
options: GRANT accepts a specific column list, so HRRole and PayrollRole each see only the exact columns their role needs, nothing else
It grants every role access to every column by default
It requires a separate masking function for every column
It only works on numeric columns, never on text columns
questions.explain: GRANT SELECT ON dbo.Employees(EmployeeId, Name, Department) TO HRRole scopes the role to exactly those columns, with Salary granted separately and only to PayrollRole.

questions.q: What does Row-Level Security (RLS) restrict, as distinguished from column-level security?
options: Which rows a query returns, rather than which columns are visible
Which stored procedures a user can execute
Which network ports the database listens on
Which backup files are retained
questions.explain: RLS means the same query, run by two different users, can return a completely different set of rows from the identical table — the classic case being multi-tenant data filtered by TenantId.

questions.q: In the RLS example, what two pieces does Row-Level Security require?
options: A security predicate function that defines the rule, and a security policy that attaches the rule to a table
A masking function and an UNMASK grant
A symmetric key and a certificate
A token vault and a mapping table
questions.explain: CREATE FUNCTION defines the predicate (comparing TenantId to SESSION_CONTEXT), and CREATE SECURITY POLICY attaches that predicate to dbo.Sales with FILTER PREDICATE.

questions.q: What is the difference between a filter predicate and a block predicate in Row-Level Security?
options: A filter predicate silently hides non-matching rows on reads; a block predicate actively rejects writes (like an INSERT) that would violate the rule
A filter predicate only applies to DELETE statements, while a block predicate only applies to SELECT statements
They are two different names for the exact same behavior
A block predicate masks column values, while a filter predicate encrypts them
questions.explain: The lesson's example adds a block predicate specifically so a user can't INSERT a row for another tenant, raising an error instead of silently filtering as a read would.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say Row-Level Security belongs in the database engine rather than being left to application code?
options: A policy enforced by the engine applies no matter what wrote the query, while application code is only as safe as every query path through it, forever
Database engines cannot run application code under any circumstances
Application code is always faster at filtering rows than the database engine
RLS is only available as an application-level feature, never as a database feature
questions.explain: The lesson draws the same point made for masking: a report, an ad-hoc tool, or a bug that forgot the filter would all bypass an application-level check, but not an engine-enforced security policy.
